title: Steroid-Sensitive Nephrotic Syndrome: First Episode, Relapses and Steroid-Sparing Agents
subject: ss-paediatric-nephrology
module: Glomerular Diseases, Nephrotic Syndrome and Nephritis

steps.say: Nephrotic syndrome in young children is defined by a triad of massive proteinuria, profound hypoalbuminemia, and generalized dependent edema.
steps.tx: Recognize the classic **Diagnostic nephrotic triad and criteria** to initiate timely pediatric evaluation. Nephrotic syndrome is formally diagnosed by heavy nephrotic-range proteinuria demonstrating urinary protein excretion exceeding 40 mg/m²/hr or a spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio > 2.0 mg/mg (or 3+ on dipstick analysis), coupled with severe hypoalbuminemia with serum albumin < 2.5 g/dL, and marked generalized dependent edema (periorbital and peripheral swelling).

vis.title: Nephrotic Syndrome Diagnostic Thresholds
rows: Produces loss of intravascular oncotic pressure
Dependent periorbital and peripheral fluid shift

steps.say: Standard primary therapy for the first presentation follows standardized international pediatric protocols using oral prednisolone.
steps.tx: Prescribe the evidence-based **IPNA/KDIGO initial steroid regimen** for presenting pediatric patients. The initial treatment protocol for a child with an inaugural episode of steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome consists of oral prednisolone administered at 60 mg/m²/day (or 2 mg/kg/day, maximum dose 60 mg) daily for 4-6 weeks, followed by alternate-day dosing at 40 mg/m² (1.5 mg/kg) on alternate days for another 4-6 weeks before stopping or gradual tapering.

nodes.label: Prednisolone 40 mg/m² alternate days x 4-6 weeks

steps.say: Daily urine monitoring allows clear distinctions between complete therapeutic remission and early clinical relapse.
steps.tx: Track daily home urinary protein to apply standard **Definitions of remission and relapse** during follow-up. Complete remission is documented when urine dipstick testing becomes trace or zero (or spot UPCR < 0.2 mg/mg) for 3 consecutive days; conversely, nephrotic relapse is diagnosed when urine dipstick shows >= 3+ protein (or spot UPCR > 2.0 mg/mg) across 3 consecutive days, typically triggered by an intercurrent viral infection.

steps.say: Specific clinical definitions distinguish children who relapse frequently from those who remain dependent on steroids.
steps.tx: Differentiate patients by established **Frequent relapser and steroid-dependent criteria** to identify candidates for steroid-sparing therapy. Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome (FRNS) is defined as experiencing >= 2 relapses within 6 months of initial response or >= 4 relapses in any 12-month period; steroid dependence (SDNS) is diagnosed when a patient develops 2 consecutive relapses during steroid taper or within 14 days of cessation.

vis.title: Subclassification of Complicated Relapsing SSNS
rows: >= 2 relapses in 6 months or >= 4 in 12-month period
Steroid toxicity risk; add steroid-sparing agent
2 consecutive relapses during taper or within 14 days
Inability to wean steroids; steroid-sparing mandatory
< 2 relapses in 6 months and < 4 in 12 months
Managed with standard short steroid courses

steps.say: Steroid-sparing agents mitigate growth failure, cataracts, and cushingoid toxicity in children with difficult courses.
steps.tx: Select appropriate second-line **Steroid-sparing agents for FRNS/SDNS** to preserve linear growth and minimize toxicity. First-line steroid-sparing options include oral levamisole (2.5 mg/kg alternate days), alkylating cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg/day for 8-12 weeks, adhering strictly to a cumulative limit 168-200 mg/kg to prevent gonadal toxicity), and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF 1200 mg/m²/day in two divided doses) to maintain sustained remission.

steps.say: Targeted B-cell depletion using rituximab offers long-term disease control in patients refractory to oral agents.
steps.tx: Deploy anti-CD20 therapy with **Rituximab in refractory SDNS** when conventional steroid-sparing therapies fail. Intravenous rituximab (administered at 375 mg/m² IV for 1-2 doses) targets selective B-cell depletion (defined by flow cytometric CD19 < 1% of total lymphocytes), demonstrating profound efficacy in inducing and maintaining long-term treatment-free remission in refractory steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome.

steps.say: Hypercoagulability and profound intravascular oncotic depletion predispose young nephrotic children to venous thrombosis.
steps.tx: Institute active precautions against **Thromboembolism prophylaxis and triggers** in severely hypoproteinemic children. Severe hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin < 2.0 g/dL), coupled with hemoconcentration, thrombocytosis, elevated fibrinogen, and marked urinary loss of antithrombin III, establishes high venous and arterial thromboembolic risk; clinicians must enforce strict avoidance of femoral venipuncture and provide prompt rehydration during intercurrent gastroenteritis.

steps.say: Impaired humoral opsonization creates heightened vulnerability to invasive encapsulated bacterial infections.
steps.tx: Recognize the pathophysiology of **Peritonitis and encapsulated bacteria** to initiate emergency antimicrobial coverage. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in nephrotic ascites is predominantly caused by encapsulated Streptococcus pneumoniae and gram-negative E. coli due to urinary loss of complement factors B and D; optimal care demands complete pneumococcal conjugate vaccination and immediate empiric intravenous cefotaxime or ceftriaxone upon clinical suspicion.
